maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RETURNING TO CAR ORDER BOOK SYSTEM

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RETURNING TO CAR ORDER BOOK SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Smith) asked me yesterday to make a statement about the suspension of the car order book in western Canada. The situation is as follows.
On December 4, 1951, the following statement was issued on behalf of the transport controller:
The transport controller today issued instructions to all railways in western Canada to discontinue operation of the car order book until July 31, 1952. This action was taken after consultation with and approval of the Canadian wheat board and the board of grain commissioners. It was considered by the two boards in a joint meeting. A very large amount of damp grain in farmers' hands and in elevators, the necessity of giving preference to certain wheat board shipping instructions, and the desirability of giving relief to those areas which have had a poor car supply, has made necessary the issuance of these instructions.
As indicated by this announcement, the suspension of the car order book was an emergency measure made necessary by the unfavourable harvest last fall and the necessity of carrying out a very unusual and complicated shipping program. For example, it was necessary after the close of navigation on the great lakes to ensure that loadings for the lakehead be confined to damp grain. It was necessary that shipments of wheat to the Pacific coast should be confined to grades of wheat which could be disposed of at the Pacific coast. It was thought advisable to route certain low grades of tough and damp wheat to interior terminals for drying. These are but examples of the unusual movements which were necessary as a result of the wide variation in grades in the 1951 crop and the fact that so much grain was harvested with an abnormally high moisture content.
It was felt by the transport controller, the wheat board and the board of grain commissioners, that a more effective shipping program from country elevators could be carried out if such shipments were based upon the co-ordinated direction of the three authorities which I have mentioned, rather than upon the ordering of cars at local delivery points by individual producers.

The abnormal circumstances which caused the transport controller to suspend the car order book still exist and the suspension remains in effect. However, I can assure the house that the suspension of the car order book will not be continued longer than necessary; and it will be noted that the order of the transport controller expires on July 31 next.

In our opinion the second amendment offered by the hon. member for Lake Centre did not extend the bill to the point where it

Foot-and-mouth disease would be of real benefit to the people within the quarantined area. I say that because as I read the bill, and as the Minister of Agriculture has explained it, at the present time the only compensation that can be paid is that paid to people whose stock is destroyed, or whose buildings, fodder or other actual property is destroyed as a result of action taken by the government.
It has been pointed out by the hon. member for Assiniboia and a great many other hon. members that there will be many losses within the quarantined area to people whose property may not be destroyed or whose herds may not be destroyed as a result of this condition. The minister indicated yesterday that that matter would have to be considered in co-operation with the provinces to decide just what might or might not have to be done.
It is our contention that this is entirely a federal responsibility, and any costs incurred as a result of quarantine placed upon an area, through the operation of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, which is a federal act, should not be passed back to the municipalities and provinces. It would cause considerable financial outlay on the part of the municipalities involved. In our opinion it is not reasonable to expect that they should have to bear the cost of something which would be the direct result of the actions of this government. Therefore we suggest to the minister that he should accept our amendment.
The amendment would add after the word "slaughtered" in subsection 1 the following words, "or to others for losses sustained." The subsection would then read:
Notwithstanding anything in the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. the Minister of Agriculture may order that fair and reasonable compensation be paid to the owners of animals slaughtered or to others for losses sustained by reason of the existence in Canada of foot-and-mouth disease . . .
And so on. In this amendment I am not suggesting that the government should be held responsible for economic losses which may occur in the livestock industry right across Canada. Some may say that under this section such action could be taken by the government. However the legislation itself is in general terms, and I have framed my amendment along the same general lines, so that it is entirely at the option of the minister so far as the payment of compensation is concerned. He may confine it to the quarantined area, just as he has stated he intends to do. He could also apply it to other parts of Canada, where we would hope the disease would not develop but where it
might develop, with the result that there would have to be quarantine provisions.
It is only fair that the legislation should be broadened so as to enable the Department of Agriculture to compensate properly. I am not so much worried about the compensation the minister will recommend under the measure. As I said before, I should think the department would pay reasonably adequate compensation, and more particularly as this may be an election year in Saskatchewan. I have never known the government to be niggardly in an election year. However that may be, I still think the principle contained in the measure is not wide enough as at present stated. Losses may be heavy for those whose herds are not directly affected, or whose herds and property might not be destroyed. Those losses should not be passed back to the municipalities or provinces, with the result that they would have to make some reasonable compensation for them.
I have asked the minister to accept this amendment, Mr. Chairman, because I realize that if I move it as a private member you will probably make the same ruling that you made with regard to an amendment moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre and rule it out of order.

speechtext: I do not think it would be wise to give the board to be set up as a result of this legislation the added enormous task involved in trying to settle all the many problems that may arise as a result of slaughtering animals in that area. maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:

speechtext:

A few minutes ago a telegram was placed on my desk giving me some details of layoffs in the packing plant. Where a province has taken steps to prevent the flow of cattle, and has thus affected the activities in these plants, the responsibility is on the province. However, in Regina where the lay-offs already number 225, the situation results from the quarantine. The suggestion that these men will be covered by unemployment insurance is not satisfactory. I am not saying that the other packing plants not in the quarantine area are a federal responsibility because the provinces have taken their own action, but the fact is that already there have been 1,500 lay-offs in the packing plants in the prairie provinces. The whole matter has many ramifications.

The tendency has been in the Canadian House of Commons for the past twenty-five years to rule out all motions purporting to give the government a direct order to do a thing which cannot be done without the expenditure of money.

speechtext: If that be so, it reveals a serious situation. Before I proceed to deal with one other phase I want to ask the minister what is the proper interpretation, based on the experience of his department.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: I come now to the question of regulations. maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: There is one other matter that really does not come within the section, but it has to do with the desire on the part of many producers of cattle throughout the country for more information than they have received so far. I have been reading one or more farm journals today, and the minimum estimated period for the continuation of the embargo is one year. If that be so, something must be done with a view to finding markets. One of the larger farm producers on the prairies-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: That is the United States embargo?

speechtext: Yes-has requested on behalf of his association that I bring to the attention of the minister a fact that he already knows, namely, that the British contract with the Argentine for the purchase of beef will expire during the coming summer, and that according to the latest report the Argentine government intends at least to double the previous price. This representative of the cattlemen has asked me to secure a statement from the minister that might bring a measure of hope to an industry which, having lost the market in the United States, is fearful today as never before. I therefore ask the minister what has been done toward re-establishing the market in Great Britain. Events of the last few days have again shown that while the proponents of agricultural trade with the United States claim it is our best market, it is subject not only to such events as have occurred recently but also to the results from time to time of change in government. I should like the minister to advise the committee what has been done and what is being done to reopen the question of the extension of the British market, which, if a surplus of beef is built up in this country, will be about the only market available for that surplus.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
There are only two reasons that I know of why we are not shipping meat to the United Kingdom. The one that is emphasized continuously is the fact that they feel they have not the dollars to buy certain food products here, one of which is meat. They will buy our wheat, for example, but they do not buy meat. They have also been buying a little cheese, but they feel they are short of dollars no matter what they might have to pay for the product. The only other reason is that they can buy meat elsewhere at lower prices than they can buy it here. I am sure my hon. friend has not in mind that we should put down the price here. Up until now we have been able to dispose of all our meat products at the prices we have been receiving. We have not taken any action which would tend to lower that price. We have to depend upon supply and demand to take care of that. So far we have been able to obtain that price. It has been said that the Argentine is going to double the price in their contract. I understand that even if they were to double it, it would still be lower than the price being paid for meat in Canada. Whether or not that is correct, it is very close to that point. Up to now there is not much which could have been said with regard to that. What may develop as a result of the difficulties we are having at the moment. I am not in a position to say.

I can assure all the members of the house that the government will be putting forth every possible effort to sell any surplus meat we have in any market that is available. We will be more anxious to sell it in the British market than in any other.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: As a matter of privilege, may I say that a moment ago I quoted from a telegram I had received. maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: Can the minister state whether the embargo imposed against Canadian meat by the United States includes cooked canned meat? In connection with this section, can he give any indication as to how long farmers in the quarantine area who have their herds destroyed will be required to remain out of business before they will be permitted to purchase healthy stock and continue in the cattle or sheep business? Will the compensation paid have any relationship to the length of time those breeders will be required to remain out of business?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
The answer to the first question is that boneless hams cured in a certain way will be admitted into the United States; the only meat admitted other than that is cooked canned meat. The two things must apply: it must be cooked and it must be canned, otherwise it is not admitted.
As to the other question, I am not sure that I fully understood it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: May I point out that a dispatch appeared in the press to the effect that the Yukon Territory has been cut off from meat supplies as a result of the embargo imposed by British Columbia. I wonder if the minister could not tell us that there are ample supplies of meat in the Peace river country contiguous to the Alaska highway. This supply is sufficient for the Yukon and Northwest territories, so there should not be any hardship in the Yukon as long as the Alaska highway is open, and it is open every day of the year.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
I noticed the article in the press this morning, Mr. Chairman, and' it was reported to me earlier that action had been taken by British Columbia to make it impossible to truck meat over the Alaska highway through their territory. I am not sure whether at this time of year much meat goes in that way, but that is a question with which my hon.
Foot-and-mouth disease friend would be more familiar than I am. If it does go up that way, it goes right by his door.
According to my experience in that part of the country, they have not been as much concerned about price as some of us are. There is nothing that prevents meat being flown from Edmonton to Whitehorse, and I am quite sure there are people there who will find a way of doing that. They fly a lot of things into that part of the country, and particularly into places like Dawson city, because at certain times of the year there has been no other way of taking in supplies. I think they will get meat in, but I can quite understand that it will be more expensive than if they could truck it. However, that is not our doing, it is the province's.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: I do not know whether the question I have is altogether relevant, but down in the maritimes the farmers were afraid that the shipment of feed grain from the western provinces might be stopped because of this foot-and-mouth disease. Can the minister state whether that would follow?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: There are no reasons why one should be concerned about that at the moment, and I doubt very much if that condition will develop. A great deal of grain can be secured outside the area. As a matter of fact, not very much feed grain would accumulate in the area under quarantine.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: The minister did not see fit to answer the question I asked him in the form in which it was asked, but perhaps he could answer another question.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member did not hear me, but I said I did not understand the question.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
I am sorry. My question was this. Can the minister give any indication as to how long farmers who have their herds destroyed must remain out of business before they will be permitted to purchase healthy stock and pasture them on the same land? That was the first part of the question. The second part was, will the compensation paid to those farmers have any relationship to the length of time they will be required to remain out of business?
The form in which I was going to ask the question now is, when the quarantine is eventually raised will that mean that there will be no restrictions whatever on the farms where this disease has been known to exist?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
I do not know whether the hon. member was in the house last night when we discussed this question. The statement I made then was to the effect that our actions in connection with the whole matter would

Foot-and-mouth disease conform very closely to those of the United States. I was not able to give any definite time, but the United States say that they will not permit our meat or livestock to enter the United States until at least sixty days after they are satisfied the disease has been entirely wiped out; that is as simply as I can put it.
If we are going to attempt to get our meat and livestock back into the United States at the earliest possible date, the more closely we follow United States practice the quicker we will gain entry to that market. Therefore, that will be approximately the practice that will be followed, and that applies to the second part of the question concerning how long these farms will be affected by regulation. They will certainly be affected until our officials are absolutely certain there is no possibility of the disease developing there again as a result of anything that has happened in the past. I am told that probably takes about sixty days. I would not like to say that is binding upon future actions.
As to the other part of the question concerning what the board will do, I am not in a position to state what they will do. All I can say is that I am quite satisfied that those who are making the estimate of the value of the animals will take into consideration all the facts that ought to be considered.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: Then the minister does not agree with the rumours or the reports that are widespread, and which I have already received in correspondence, that because the virus may remain in the soil that land should not be pastured for a period of at least one year after the all-clear is given. Is there any truth in that rumour? I think that is what the hon. member had in mind.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
I am fold that our officials do not feel that that is necessary, but we should not like to be bound in certain cases to not putting on some special restrictions. As a matter of fact, what they do is put animals on the land. We actually secure animals, and when we get to a certain stage in the program we put those animals on the land and we have veterinarians check them all the time over a certain period of time. If it is then found that the disease does not develop, it is taken for granted that it is not there.
Section 2, subsection 2, agreed to.

speechtext: Before you call clause 3, Mr. Chairman-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
-I have a further amendment which I wish to suggest as subclause 3 of clause 2 of the bill. As I said last night,

when we were discussing the matter in the house with the minister, I feel that this bill overlooks an important aspect of this whole problem, namely the need for some payment or some consideration to those 2,000 farmers or more within that quarantined area who are now affected by the quarantine regulations. I had asked the minister if stock would be permitted to move within the quarantine area from the farmer's homestead site to the summer pasture, and the minister said that would not be allowed. I then asked him if the government were considering-and I think this is an extremely important matter-some assistance to the 2,000 farmers many of whom will have to provide feed for their livestock on their homestead sites, throughout the early part or perhaps even all of the summer. I think that is one important aspect of the matter that the government has entirely overlooked. I asked the minister if he was going to solicit from the government of Saskatchewan any financial aid in moving feed and fodder into that quarantined area, and the minister replied as follows, as reported at page 129 of Hansard:
I am not saying I am going to solicit it. I say it will be discussed with them. I do not know what the outcome of the discussion will be.
From that statement it seems fairly clear to me that the minister is going to attempt in Regina to unload at least part of the government's responsibility in dealing with this disease in that quarantined area. There is going to be terrific expense for the 2,000 or more farmers within that area who will have used up their winter supply of fodder in the spring and who will have to bring feed and fodder from outside of the area in order to maintain their cattle throughout the summer months. I believe this is a federal responsibility because of the regulations that have been applied to that area. These regulations stem directly from a federal act, the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. When this government applies those regulations, as it must, then I think the government should see to it that any undue hardship, caused to farmers within that area because of the disease and because of the regulations, is properly dealt with. Apart from the problem of compensating those farmers whose livestock are slaughtered, I think there is no problem which is more important and naturally it is a matter which will affect far more farmers than are affected by the compensation provided in this act. In the hope that the minister and the government will accept this responsibility I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), the following amendment:
That clause 2 of Bill 7 be amended by adding thereto the following subclause (3):

",R' The Minister of Agriculture may also order and make provision for the supplying of feed and fodder to the owners of animals in any area quarantined by reason of the existence in Canada of foot-and-mouth disease."
That amendment, Mr. Chairman, would make it clear that this is the federal government's responsibility and that, under this legislation, the minister would have power to deal with, order, and make provision for the supplying of feed and fodder. It is different from the last amendment which was suggested when the minister raised the objection that the board of valuators already has enough to do and that to give further powers to it would make it difficult for that board to function. This additional subclause I propose having inserted in clause 2 of the bill would not give to the board any further powers or duties but would give the Minister of Agriculture himself more power.
I do not think the Minister of Agriculture is a man who in the past has shunned the accepting of additional authority and power. He seems to like to deal with as many phases as possible with respect to agriculture, particularly in western Canada. While we do not always agree with what the minister does when he gets some of these powers, I have seldom heard anyone objecting when the minister is given additional power. I would therefore ask the minister to consider whether or not this further subclause might be accepted so that he would have the power to order and to make provision for the supplying of feed and fodder throughout the summer months within that quarantined area. I believe it will be an important problem. I believe the minister should have this power. With such power I believe he would be in a position to render a real service to all the farmers within that quarantined area.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
Just to keep the record straight, I think what I said last evening was something to the effect that right at the present moment the farmer would not be permitted to move his livestock from his home farm to a pasture which may be two, three or four miles away. If the pasture is contiguous to the land he is operating otherwise or where his home is, of course he can move them from one farm to another. But that is not saying what we will be able to do in June. It is not saying what he will be able to do in the early part of May. At this moment I am not in a position to say what the position will be then. Many of these restrictions which we now have on may be off, and the farmers may be able to do something quite different from what they are able to do at this moment. I am therefore not in a position to judge with regard to that matter.
Foot-and-mouth disease
I would, however, point out that anything which has been suggested by the hon. member as being possible under this proposed amendment could have been done under the amendment which we just declared to be out of order. In other words, in substance they really mean the same thing, namely that the minister can do nearly anything he likes with regard to the expenditure of money and with regard to what he spends the money for. I am quite sure that if the one is out of order, the other is also. The one has already been declared out of order. To come to the practical question, I think all we have to do during this session is to keep on wasting as much time on every other piece of legislation as we have on this one up to date, and we will still be here to deal with any of the things that happen any time during the period that this area is under quarantine.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: Before you make your ruling, Mr. Chairman, I wish to say I resent the insinuation of the minister that members of parliament have been wasting the time of the house in discussing a matter so important as compensation for this dread disease. maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: What a man!

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: The minister has said that it may not be necessary to have power like this, even though he should accept the amendment. It would be a service to the farmers within that area, and they would appreciate the minister's accepting this suggestion, particularly if they knew that the Minister of Agriculture was taking the responsibility of assisting them in their great need.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to review any of the facts in connection with this bill. But certainly the events of the last two or three days have revealed a situation serious, indeed tragic, in its consequences, and fantastic by reason of the fact that the government failed to act last November, when it should have acted.
It is strange that, realizing the terrible danger of this virus, realizing too how similar were the symptoms to those of the foot-and-mouth disease, the only diagnosis taken was a more or less superficial one, and one which did not take into consideration the need for the fullest, most exacting and most careful examination so as to give the assurance that the disease was not in fact the foot-and-mouth disease.

The hon. member for Brant-Wentworth (Mr. Charlton) has shown conclusively that had the government acted properly it would have exhausted every possibility, instead of relying upon agreement, however general -it may have been, among several veterinarians, none of whom took the tests which resulted finally in the discovery of the disease. How terrible the consequences will be of the failure of the government to act will become apparent only with the passing months. Already however there have been results indicating why it is that every precaution should have been taken, and why delays from November 17, on, cannot be excused.
Last night the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) read from the Year Book of Agriculture, a publication of the United States department of agriculture. I now refer to page 268 of the same publication where it says that in the United States extreme caution is used in making a diagnosis. It there refers to the terrible danger to the economy of livestock production when there is failure of a government to act.
However the government may endeavour to excuse delay, the unfolding of the record reveals apathy, postponement and, indeed, indifference to the tremendous danger and the awfulness of the probabilities connected with incorrect diagnosis, or the failure to recognize the difference between vesicular stomatitis and the disease in question.
However, all this is past. What we are now concerned with is to give assurance to those affected within the area-and all of us hope the condition may be restricted to that area-that everything possible will be done for them. One must keep in mind, however, the fact that animals were in the stockyards in Regina for a period of time under a state of semi-quarantine. All of us know that the pens in question are adjacent to the general yards; and the possibility that the disease may have spread is one that deserves at least the closest examination and the fullest investigation, particularly in respect of the destination of each and every one of those cattle.
In my view the bill is misnamed. We see it is entitled "an act for the control and extirpation of foot-and-mouth disease". It is nothing of the sort. It is an act for the payment of damages resulting to individuals in consequence of the destruction of their herds or any of their animals, with a view to controlling and extirpating the disease.
What we are now trying to do is to give proper compensation. Last night I moved an amendment which I realized would be out of order, were the minister to say that it would mean an extra expenditure on the part of
Foot-and-mouth disease the crown over and above that comprehended by the legislation. Very properly the minister admitted that such was the case. Up until that moment there were many who felt that the compensation would be greater than the commercial value, plus the allowances for which provision is made under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act.
When the minister made that statement, however, it established absolutely the contention of those of us on this side of the house whose view it was that the provisions of the measure offered by the government would not cover the economic value of the loss the farmers would suffer in consequence of the destruction of their herds. As hon. members have said this afternoon, however much we want to compensate the farmers within that area for their losses, both direct and indirect-and I think Canadians generally want to give that compensation-no private member in the house may so move. That is provided under our constitutional procedure.
In order to bring the matter to a head, and because it is clear to me that the farmers who suffer damage are not going to receive compensation on the basis of their economic losses, or the economic value of the animals destroyed, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth (Mr. Charlton):
That Bill 7 be not now read the third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of reconsidering an addition to section 2, subsection 1, to provide that in no case shall such compensation be less than the economic value of the animal or animals at the time the said disease was diagnosed.
I submit, on the authorities, that this kind of amendment has been moved frequently in the past. It gives the house an opportunity of making the recommendation that consideration be given in committee of the whole to assuring that in the event that the consideration becomes acceptable, the economic value of the animals destroyed will be paid, instead of placing the farmers in the position of relying upon the nebulous expression, "fair and reasonable valuation", an expression which is capable of so many interpretations.
The minister himself is reported at page 43 of Hansard as having used these words:
The act now says "fair and reasonable value," which could be even higher than the commercial value, or lower as the case may be.
But we want to give the assurance that the farmer whose animals are destroyed will receive compensation for the economic value, which includes within its terms those intangibles to which reference has already been made and which are not by any stretch of the imagination comprised within the words "fair and reasonable value".

It seems to me we would be doing a service to the farmers of Canada if we concluded this debate shortly and let the minister deal with the situation. This morning I wrote a letter to the only member of the Manitoba legislature whom I know personally, and I should like to place it on the record. It reads:
Ottawa, March 5, 1952
Mr. John Pitt,
Legislative Assembly,
Winnipeg, Manitoba.
Dear Mr. Pitt:
For the last two days here in the House of Commons, the time has been solely taken up with the foot-and-mouth disease, and I presume it will go on all day today.

Personally, I feel this may have been warranted at the time it was done, but I hope that the Manitoba government is giving serious consideration to having this embargo removed.

Regina, and there is also what is called a buffer zone, taking in another 15 miles around this. Mr. Gardiner, I understand, is flying west at the end of the week to discuss this problem with the officials of the Saskatchewan government, on an invitation from them, and I am sure that if the Manitoba government requested, he would also stop in Winnipeg to discuss this very important problem.
I do not need to explain any further the position that many of us in Saskatchewan are placed in by the Manitoba embargo. I am sure you know and realize what the facts are.
Trusting you will do what is possible regarding this matter, I remain
Yours sincerely,

Mr. Speaker, before the house gives final consent to the passage of the bill I should like to make a few remarks, following which I shall move

an amendment. I believe no real purpose can be accomplished at this time by going over all the events leading up to the introduction of the present bill. Although I believe there has been the greatest negligence, and an indication of absolute incompetence on the part of departmental officials, the farmers affected throughout Canada are now interested in what kind of treatment they will receive, if the disease should break out in their herds.
Why it took so long for departmental officials to cope with the disease, I cannot say. Perhaps they thought that the risk in announcing that the disease might be foot-and-mouth disease was so grave that they then engaged in one of the greatest gambles this country has ever known by delaying so long making the proper tests in order to ascertain the nature of the ailment.
Not only in order that the farmers within the quarantined area should receive some additional consideration, but for the further purpose of protecting livestock herds which might be affected by the disease at some time in the future, I feel parliament should provide assistance to those people to maintain their herds until such time as the quarantine may be lifted.
In addition, the picture today for farmers across Canada outside the quarantined area looks very discouraging, indeed. Because of the provincial embargoes, and because of the disease itself, involving as it does the loss of the United States market, there has been a drastic fall in hog and cattle prices in many provinces over the last week. The Calgary Herald of March 1 reports that in the preceding week-that is last week-feeder steers and heifers on the Calgary market dropped by $5 per hundredweight. Bulls dropped $8 per hundredweight, while feeder steers going into the killing pen dropped from $6 to $7 per hundredweight. In spite of the floor the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) placed under hog prices, those prices dropped in Calgary last week to $22 a hundredweight for grade A, while the price of sows dropped to 11 cents per pound, live weight.
The government should consider the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease as a national emergency, an emergency just as great as the emergency that faced the prairie farmers last fall when they were unable to deliver their grain to the elevators. When at that time the government was faced with transportation difficulties it had the foresight to appoint a controller. For that action I offer them my praise. Up until that time many members on the opposition side of the house- and there have been some complaints since-
Foot-and-mouth disease complained that the Canadian Pacific Railway was not distributing box cars on a fair basis. However, when the controller was appointed he was able to direct the railway to allocate those cars more fairly.
I say that at this time the cattle industry in Canada needs a controller; the hog industry needs a controller. The government has floor price legislation, but we need a controller in Canada to direct the packing houses to pay nothing less than the government's announced floor prices. So I trust the government may yet consider the appointment of a controller and the establishment of fair cattle and hog floor prices throughout Canada. I would hope that it would give the controller the necessary power to direct packers in Canada from one coast to the other to pay adequate floor prices to the producers. Packers should not be permitted to use the foot-and-mouth disease as an excuse for lowering the price of hogs to a point below the floor price announced by the government, so that they may gain a large speculative profit when the transportation restrictions are removed.
As I have repeated on a number of occasions, one of the most important problems and one of the chief worries of the farmers within the quarantined area is the provision of feed and fodder to maintain their herds throughout the summer months when, ordinarily, those herds would be moved to pastures off the farm sites. Because I believe such action should be taken, and because I believe parliament should express an opinion as to whether the government should take such action, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), the following amendment:
That Bill 7 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house for the purpose of reconsidering an amendment thereto which would give the Minister of Agriculture authority to order and make provision for the supplying of feed and fodder to the owners of animals in any area quarantined by reason of the existence in Canada of foot-and-mouth disease.
If the government adopted the suggestion contained in the amendment the minister would be in a position not only to provide feed and fodder within the present quarantined area but, should the disease spread to other areas, the minister would be in a position to provide feed and fodder for the affected herds within such other areas.
In view of the fact that the cost of carrying out the suggestion would not be great and the further fact that this is a national emergency during which the farmers should be assured that the government will stand by them when they face hardship in feeding

I have some doubts as to whether the amendment is within the scope of the resolution, which is in these words:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure for the control and extirpation of foot-and-mouth disease and to provide in connection therewith for the payment of compensation, out of moneys appropriated by parliament, to the owners of animals slaughtered, and also in respect of any buildings, fodder, grain or other things ordered to be destroyed.
I have some hesitancy in allowing the amendment to stand.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. As you know, I am not an authority on the rules of parliament. As I understood the resolution preceding this bill, it indicated that the government intended to do certain things to deal with the outbreak of this disease and the results therefrom. The bill provides for certain compensation, but this amendment would give the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the government the further power to provide compensation in the way of feed and fodder to farmers within the area affected by this disease.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the point raised by the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue) answers the question raised by Your Honour. The resolution preceding the bill contemplated among other things that compensation would be paid in respect of fodder, grain or other things ordered to be destroyed. Surely what my colleague is asking for is a form of compensation for feed and fodder in the areas where it is needed as a result of the minister exercising the powers set out in the bill. I recognize readily that it is a difficult point, perhaps a borderline case, but it does seem to me that as this amendment relates to feed and fodder it comes within the scope of the resolution which had royal recognition.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: I have listened to what the hon. members have said. I have reread the resolution and I have reread this bill. The bill refers to the slaughtering of animals and to compensation to owners of animals so slaughtered. In my opinion the amendment goes far beyond the provisions of the resolution and of the bill and for that reason I shall have to rule it out of order.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the amendment moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) is out of order, I am quite sure that the amendment which I am going to propose will be in order because it deals exactly with the bill. I shall not take any time to cover ground that has been covered so well already by so many hon. members. This matter of providing compensation of some kind to people directly affected, although their stock may not have been destroyed, is most important to the people in that area. We hope that it may not happen, but if this disease should break out in any other area and quarantine be made necessary this matter will be of great importance to the people in such areas. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That Bill 7 be not now read1 a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house for the purpose of reconsidering an amendment thereto which would provide for the payment of compensation to any persons suffering losses of income by reason of the existence in Canada of foot-and-mouth disease.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
It seems to me that this amendment also is beyond the scope of the resolution. The amendment asks that the bill be referred back to the committee of the whole house for the purpose of reconsidering an amendment thereto. Under the provisions of the amendment any person, whether he be a farmer, whether he be a workman, whether he be, as someone has suggested, a lawyer, no matter who he was, if his income was affected as a result of this disease he would be compensated. I do not think I can allow the amendment to stand as it is far beyond the scope of the resolution and the terms of the bill. I must declare the amendment out of order.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.
